question: Chemicals can be found in almost all strategic value chains. They are essential for more than 95 % of manufactured goods. The European Union is the second largest producer of chemicals. However, competition from China in particular reduced the EU’s share of global sales from 27 % in 2002 to 14 % in 2022. Over the same period, the share of EU chemical companies’ spending on new projects in Asia increased by 50 %.

In 2012, the EU chemical industry’s global trade surplus was almost EUR 50 billion1, compared to just EUR 2.5 billion in 2022. According to figures from the European Chemical Industry Council, in the first nine months of 2023, EU chemicals production fell by 10.6 % in comparison to 20222.

This further decline is attributed to the war in Ukraine, high energy costs, rising interest rates, inflation, but also the deadweight effect of the IRA on the US chemical industry3. What urgent solutions will the Commission put in place to defend the European chemical industry, one of its key economic sectors?
‘Nouveau record pour la chimie européenne’, L’Usine Nouvelle, 14 April 2013. ‘La mutation forcée de la chimie européenne’, Les Échos, 14 December 2023. Inflation Reduction Act.
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.4.2024) The EU chemical industry is at the heart of EU’s strategic value chains. Many goods, such as semiconductors, pharmaceuticals, and electronics rely on chemicals.

In the face of rising energy costs, of sometimes unfair competition from third countries, and of the vital need for a strong chemical industry in Europe for the twin transition and resilience, an integrated approach for the chemical industry is needed. In 2023, the Commission co-created with stakeholders the transition pathway for the chemical industry1.

It highlights about 190 actions to be co-implemented with the EU chemical industry and Member States to deliver on EU’s ambition and achieve the twin transition of the chemical industry. In addition, the Commission extended provisions in the Temporary Crisis and Transition Framework2, allowing Member States to grant limited aid amounts and aid to compensate for high energy prices until 30 June 2024.

EU funds also provide substantial support to the chemical industry. For instance, the Innovation Fund is financing the Kairos project3 to build the largest carbon capture and storage petrochemicals hub in Antwerp. Besides, regulatory predictability and coherence are required for the chemicals sector to invest in decarbonisation. This applies in particular to the implementation of the EU Emissions Trading System4.

In addition, the political agreement reached between co-legislators on the Net-Zero Industry Act5 includes the possibility to support and scale up decarbonisation projects in energy intensive industries, including chemicals, through faster and simpler permitting procedures.
